meta.provenance: Concepts and trap structures derived from KMF/Gremlin's GRE source set; every stem, all numbers, all options, all explanations and all figures are original. No source text or artwork reproduced. Several single-answer sources were recast into numeric-entry and multiple-answer form, since the Coordinate Geometry source pool skews to MCQ and quantitative comparison.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, what is the x-intercept of the line that passes through (4, -3) and is perpendicular to the line 6x - 2y = 7?
questions.explanation: First get the slope of the given line: 6x - 2y = 7 becomes 2y = 6x - 7, so y = 3x - 7/2 and the slope is 3. A perpendicular line has the negative reciprocal slope, -1/3. Through (4, -3): y + 3 = -(1/3)(x - 4), which expands to y = -(1/3)x + 4/3 - 3 = -(1/3)x - 5/3. Setting y = 0 gives (1/3)x = -5/3, so x = -5.
questions.trap: Students build the correct line and then report -5/3, its y-intercept, instead of its x-intercept. The x-intercept is where y = 0, not where x = 0, and on this line those are -5 and -5/3 respectively.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, the graph of y = f(x) is a line. If f(3) = 5/2, f(7) = 1/2 and f(11) = -3/2, what is the value of f(1)? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explanation: Because the graph is a line, the rate of change is constant. From x = 3 to x = 7 the output falls from 5/2 to 1/2, a drop of 2 over a run of 4, so the slope is -1/2. Checking against the third value: from x = 7 to x = 11 the run is 4 and the drop is again 2, confirming the slope. Moving from x = 3 back to x = 1 is a run of -2, so the output rises by (-1/2)(-2) = 1. Therefore f(1) = 5/2 + 1 = 7/2.
questions.trap: Students apply the slope in the wrong direction, subtracting 1 instead of adding it and answering 3/2. Going from x = 3 down to x = 1 moves left, and on a line of negative slope moving left raises the output.

questions.question:
The figure shows a line through the origin in the xy-plane making an angle of 30 degrees with the positive x-axis. The point (a, b) lies on this line with a > 0.
Column A: |a|
Column B: |b|
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 260" width="320" height="260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#1f2937"/></marker></defs><line x1="26.0" y1="130.0" x2="294.0" y2="130.0" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="160.0" y1="225.7" x2="160.0" y2="34.3" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="290.0" y="146.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">x</text><text x="167.0" y="45.3" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">y</text><text x="147.0" y="145.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">O</text><line x1="60.5" y1="187.4" x2="259.5" y2="72.6" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="226.3" cy="91.7" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="222.3" y="79.7" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="middle">(a, b)</text><path d="M 202.1 130.0 A 42.1 42.1 0 0 0 196.5 108.9" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="215.5" y="114.7" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">30 degrees</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: A line at 30 degrees to the positive x-axis is much closer to horizontal than to vertical, so as you travel out along it you move farther sideways than upward. Put concretely, the angle the line makes with the x-axis is 30 degrees while the angle it makes with the y-axis is 60 degrees, and the coordinate measured along the direction the line hugs more closely is the larger one. Numerically the ratio b/a is the tangent of 30 degrees, which is about 0.58, so b is only a little over half of a. Since a > 0 and the point is above the axis, |a| is greater than |b|.
questions.trap: Students assume a point on a slanted line has coordinates of roughly equal size and answer C. That happens only at 45 degrees. At 30 degrees the run outpaces the rise by nearly two to one.

questions.question:
In the xy-plane, the point (3, 1) is a vertex of a square whose sides have length 4.

Which of the following could be the vertex diagonally opposite (3, 1)?

Indicate all such points.
questions.explanation: In a square of side 4, the diagonal has length 4 times sqrt(2), which is about 5.66. The square may be tilted any way at all, so the opposite vertex can be any point at exactly that distance from (3, 1). Checking the options by their offsets from (3, 1): (7, 5) is (4, 4) away, a distance of sqrt(32) = 4*sqrt(2), so it qualifies; (-1, -3) is (-4, -4) away, also 4*sqrt(2); (7, -3) is (4, -4) away, again 4*sqrt(2). Meanwhile (3, 5) is (0, 4) away, a distance of 4, and (7, 1) is (4, 0) away, also 4 — those are side lengths, not diagonals. And (8, 1) is 5 away, which is neither.
questions.trap: Options D and E sit exactly 4 units from the given vertex, so students who are hunting for 'the other corner' grab them. A distance of 4 marks an adjacent vertex along a side; the diagonally opposite corner is farther, at 4*sqrt(2).

questions.question: In the xy-plane, circle C is centered at (0, 5) and passes through the point (3, 1). What is the area of circle C?
questions.explanation: The radius is the distance from the center to the given point. The horizontal gap is 3 - 0 = 3 and the vertical gap is 1 - 5 = -4, so r^2 = 3^2 + (-4)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 and r = 5. The area is pi times r^2, which is 25 pi. Note that r^2 is all the area formula needs, so the square root step can be skipped entirely.
questions.trap: Students square the center's y-coordinate instead of the vertical gap, computing 3^2 + 5^2 = 34 and answering 34 pi. The radius depends on the difference between the coordinates, 1 - 5 = -4, not on the coordinate 5 itself.

questions.question:
In the xy-plane, for each positive integer n the point P(n) is (n, 3), and d(n) is the distance from the origin to P(n).
Column A: d(12)
Column B: sqrt(153)
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: The point P(12) is (12, 3). Its distance from the origin is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 12 and 3, so d(12) = sqrt(12^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(144 + 9) = sqrt(153). That is exactly Column B, so the two quantities are equal. There is no need to evaluate the root.
questions.trap: Students simplify sqrt(153) as though 153 were a perfect square, or add the legs to get 15 and compare 15 with the roughly 12.4 that sqrt(153) evaluates to, choosing A. Squaring Column B returns 153, which is precisely 144 + 9.

questions.question: The figure shows a quadrilateral in the xy-plane with vertices (2, 10), (10, 4), (6, 0) and (0, 6). What is the area of the quadrilateral?

questions.explanation: Enclose the quadrilateral in the square running from x = 0 to x = 10 and from y = 0 to y = 10, which has area 100. Each of the four vertices lands on a different side of that square, so the leftover area is exactly four right triangles, one in each corner. At the corner (0, 10) the legs run from (0, 6) up to (0, 10), a length of 4, and from (0, 10) across to (2, 10), a length of 2, giving area 4. At (10, 10) the legs are 8 and 6, giving area 24. At (10, 0) the legs are 4 and 4, giving area 8. At (0, 0) the legs are 6 and 6, giving area 18. The corners total 4 + 24 + 8 + 18 = 54, so the quadrilateral has area 100 - 54 = 46.
questions.trap: Students eyeball the shape as roughly a 10-by-10 square with the corners shaved and guess 80, or they pair up sides that look parallel and apply the trapezoid formula. No two sides of this quadrilateral are parallel, and none is horizontal or vertical, so only the enclose-and-subtract route is reliable.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, circle C has center (2, 3), and the point (7, 15) lies on circle C. What is the slope of the line tangent to circle C at (7, 15)?
questions.explanation: A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency. The radius runs from (2, 3) to (7, 15), so its slope is (15 - 3)/(7 - 2) = 12/5. The tangent's slope is the negative reciprocal of that, which is -5/12.
questions.trap: Students compute the radius slope 12/5 and stop there, answering D, or they negate without inverting and answer -12/5. Perpendicular slopes must multiply to -1, and (12/5)(-5/12) = -1 while (12/5)(-12/5) does not.

questions.question:
In the xy-plane, line L has equation 2y - 3 = 3x + 9.
Column A: the y-coordinate at which L crosses the y-axis
Column B: the x-coordinate at which L crosses the x-axis
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Solve for y first: 2y = 3x + 12, so y = (3/2)x + 6. The y-intercept is then 6, read straight off the constant. For the x-intercept set y = 0: 0 = (3/2)x + 6 gives (3/2)x = -6 and x = -4. Comparing 6 with -4, Column A is greater.
questions.trap: Students mishandle the sign when solving 0 = (3/2)x + 6, getting x = 4 instead of -4 and concluding Column B wins. The line has positive slope and a positive y-intercept, so it must cross the x-axis to the left of the origin.

The figure shows segment AB in the xy-plane, with A(1, 10) and B(1, 16), together with triangle DEF, whose vertices are D(-5, 2), E(9, 4) and F(7, 2).

Which of the following segments have length 10?

Indicate all such segments.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

questions.explanation: Work out each distance from its horizontal and vertical gaps. From A(1, 10) to D(-5, 2) the gaps are -6 and -8, giving sqrt(36 + 64) = 10. From A to E(9, 4) the gaps are 8 and -6, giving sqrt(64 + 36) = 10 again. From A to F(7, 2) the gaps are 6 and -8, giving 10 once more, so A is exactly 10 units from all three vertices. From B(1, 16) the picture is different: to D the gaps are -6 and -14, giving sqrt(232); to E they are 8 and -12, giving sqrt(208); to F they are 6 and -14, giving sqrt(232). None of those is 10.
questions.trap: Students judge by eye from the figure and mark BD or BF because those look comparable to AD. Every one of the six distances has to be computed; B sits 6 units above A, which pushes all three of its distances past 14.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, line m passes through the point (6, 6) and is perpendicular to the line x + y = 2. The point (a, b) lies on line m and is halfway between (6, 6) and the line x + y = 2. What is the value of a + b?
questions.explanation: The line x + y = 2 rearranges to y = -x + 2, so its slope is -1 and any perpendicular line has slope 1. Line m therefore passes through (6, 6) with slope 1, which makes it y = x. Line m meets x + y = 2 where x + x = 2, that is at x = 1 and y = 1, the point (1, 1). Being halfway between (6, 6) and the line means being the midpoint of (6, 6) and (1, 1), which is (3.5, 3.5). So a + b = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7.
questions.trap: Students give line m the slope -1, copying x + y = 2 instead of taking its negative reciprocal; that line is parallel to x + y = 2 and never meets it, so there is no foot to measure from. Others locate the foot (1, 1) correctly but then report a + b for the foot itself, answering 2, rather than for the midpoint (3.5, 3.5).

questions.question:
The figure shows circle P, centered at (0, 0) with radius 5, and circle Q, centered at (8, 0) with radius 3, in the xy-plane. At how many points do the two circles intersect?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

questions.explanation: Compare the distance between the centers with the two radii. The centers are (0, 0) and (8, 0), so they are 8 units apart. The radii sum to 5 + 3 = 8, exactly the distance between the centers. That is the borderline case: the circles touch at a single point, the one lying on the segment joining the centers, namely (5, 0). If the centers were closer than 8 the circles would cross twice; farther than 8 and they would miss entirely.
questions.trap: The figure is not drawn to scale and shows the two circles overlapping, so students read two crossings straight off the picture and answer C; others simply assume that two distinct circles either miss entirely or cross twice. When the sum of the radii equals the distance between the centers, the circles are externally tangent and meet at exactly one point.
